newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian parties open peaceful election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian parties open peaceful election campaign.

text.p: Indonesia's three legal political parties hit the hustings on Sunday at the start of a month-long general election campaign to woo nearly 125 million voters in the world's fourth most populous nation.
The country's leaders appealed for a peaceful campaign, and a survey of major cities around the nation of 200 million people produced no reports of trouble.
President Suharto's eldest daughter, businesswoman Siti Hardyanti "Tutut" Rukmana, kicked off the campaign of the ruling Golkar at Semarang in volatile central Java with a call for calm.
"We must be watchful of security. We must be orderly," she told about 10,000 people at a fairground in the industrial port city. Tutut is also one of seven chairmen of Golkar.
Populous central Java was hit by pre-campaign violence in recent weeks, primarily between supporters of Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP).

Golkar, the PPP and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), the only three groups legally permitted to contest the May 29 local and national elections, have agreed to campaign each day in separate areas of the country.

On Sunday, Golkar was campaigning across Java and in the remote Mulukus and Irian Jaya in far the east of the archipelago of more than 17,000 islands sprawled across the erquator. It is seeking more than 70 percent of the vote after taking 68 percent in the last elections in 1992.
The PPP, which won 17 percent in 1992, was campaigning in Sumatra, the resort island of Bali and its adjacent Nusa Tenggara islands.

The PDI, badly split since its leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted by government-backed rebels last year, was seeking voter backing in Kalimantan on Borneo island and Sulawesi. It took 15 percent in 1992.

Reuter correspondent Jim Della-Giacoma reported from Semarang that about 10,000 people were at the fairground, where Tutut also called on the electorate not to spoil their ballots or boycott the polls.
"We must all join in the general election because it ensures the future of the nation. You must not join 'golput' (spoil ballots)," Tutut said.

In the north Sumatran city and trading centre of Medan, Reuters correspondent Raju Gopalakrishnan reported about 5,000 people turned out to hear PPP leader Ismail Hasan Metareum list what he said were four basic rights: education, security, political activity and employment.

"These are four essential rights of the people," he said. He told Reuters he expected the party to win 100 of the 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives, compared with 62 in 1992 and a peak of 99 in 1977.
The remaining 75 seats in the 500-member house are alloted to the military which does not vote.
Dozens of children milled around at the Medan rally, some with their heads shaved into green-dyed stars for the symbol and colour of the PPP.
Indonesian markets were jittery last week on fears of possible campaign violence. The rupiah dropped 20 points to 2,440.50 to the dollar before moving back to 2,436 by Saturday.
The Jakarta Stock Exchange was little changed on Friday, with the composite index closing at 652.4 points, but brokers attributed some profit-taking to election nerves.

"The crucial point is Sunday and Monday. People are looking at the start of the campaign which should give indications whether the authorities have things under control," a foreign exchange dealer said.
